title: Software development amortization rules under Section 174
description: Section 174 software development costs were amortized over 5 years (domestic) or 15 (foreign) for 2022–2024; Section 174A restores domestic expensing.
summary: Under Section 174, U.S. businesses had to capitalize software development costs and amortize them over 5 years (domestic) or 15 years (foreign) for tax years beginning 2022–2024. For tax years beginning after December 31, 2024, new Section 174A restores immediate deduction of domestic software development costs, while foreign software development remains subject to 15-year amortization.

body.text: Under Section 174, U.S. businesses had to capitalize software development costs and amortize them over 5 years (domestic) or 15 years (foreign) for tax years beginning 2022–2024. For tax years beginning after December 31, 2024, new Section 174A restores immediate deduction of domestic software development costs, while foreign software development remains subject to 15-year amortization.

Law and guidance reflected: Internal Revenue Code as amended through Pub. L. 119-21 (July 4, 2025), Rev. Proc. 2025-28 (released August 28, 2025, modifying Rev. Proc. 2025-23), Notice 2023-63, Notice 2024-12, and FASB Accounting Standards Update (ASU) 2025-06. This report is informational and is not legal or tax advice.
1. The TCJA Capitalization Regime (Tax Years Beginning 2022–2024)
1.1 Effective date and the end of immediate deduction

The Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (TCJA, Pub. L. 115-97, § 13206(a)) amended Section 174 for amounts paid or incurred in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021, eliminating the option to currently deduct research or experimental expenditures under former Section 174(a) and requiring instead that specified research or experimental (SRE) expenditures be charged to capital account and amortized over fixed statutory periods. Under TCJA § 13206(b), the mandatory transition from immediate expensing (or elective 60-month amortization under former Section 174(b)) to mandatory capitalization and amortization was designated by statute as a change in method of accounting initiated by the taxpayer, made with the consent of the Secretary of the Treasury, and applied on a cut-off basis for SRE expenditures paid or incurred in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021, with no IRC Section 481(a) adjustment permitted or required for costs paid or incurred in prior taxable years.
1.2 Software development is treated as research or experimental expenditure

Section 174(c)(3), as enacted by the TCJA, expressly provides that for purposes of Section 174, any amount paid or incurred in connection with the development of any software shall be treated as a research or experimental expenditure. IRS Notice 2023-63 (section 2.02(3) and section 4.02(2)) confirms that, for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021, software development expenditures paid or incurred by a taxpayer during a taxable year in connection with the taxpayer's trade or business are SRE expenditures subject to mandatory capitalization and amortization. Following the enactment of Pub. L. 119-21 in 2025, this identical statutory rule classifying software development costs as research or experimental expenditures is codified in Section 174A(d) with respect to domestic research or experimental expenditures, while remaining in Section 174(c)(3) for foreign research or experimental expenditures.

Section 12 of Notice 2023-63 (as clarified by Notice 2024-12) declares section 5 of Rev. Proc. 2000-50—which previously permitted taxpayers to treat costs to develop computer software in a manner analogous to former Section 174(a) current deductions or former Section 174(b) 60-month ratable amortization—obsolete for amounts paid or incurred in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021. Only section 5 of Rev. Proc. 2000-50 was rendered obsolete, leaving the revenue procedure's definitions and rules regarding acquired computer software intact.
1.3 What counts as software development

Under section 5.02(1) of Notice 2023-63, "computer software" is broadly defined (consistent with section 2 of Rev. Proc. 2000-50 and Treas. Reg. § 1.197-2(c)(4)(iv)) to include any program or routine (that is, any sequence of machine-readable code) that is designed to cause a computer to perform a desired function or set of functions, and the documentation required to describe and maintain that program or routine, including system documentation, user manuals, and flowcharts, as well as upgrades and enhancements. Under section 5.03 of Notice 2023-63, activities that are treated as software development for purposes of Section 174 include:

items: planning the development of the computer software (or the upgrades and enhancements to such software), including identifying and documenting the software requirements;
designing the computer software (or the upgrades and enhancements to such software);
building a model of the computer software (or the upgrades and enhancements to such software);
writing source code and converting it to machine-readable code;

testing the computer software (or the upgrades and enhancements to such software) and making necessary modifications to address defects identified during testing, up until the point in time the software is placed in service or ready for sale or licensing; and
in the case of computer software developed to be sold or licensed to others (or upgrades and enhancements to such software), production of the product master(s).

body.text: The statutory and administrative endpoint of capitalization-triggering development activities differs depending on the intended use of the software. For computer software developed by a taxpayer for use in its own trade or business (internal-use software), software development activities run until the point in time the software is placed in service (Notice 2023-63, section 5.03(5)(a)). For computer software developed for sale or licensing to others, software development activities continue until technological feasibility has been established, product masters have been produced, and the software is ready for sale or licensing to others (section 5.03(5)(b) and (6)). Under section 5.02(2) of Notice 2023-63, upgrades and enhancements—defined as modifications to existing computer software that result in additional functionality (enabling the software to perform tasks that it was previously incapable of performing) or that materially increase the speed or efficiency of the software—are treated as software development on the same principles. The rules of Notice 2023-63 section 5 apply equally to computer software developed for the taxpayer's own internal trade or business use and computer software developed for sale or licensing to external customers.

Section 5.05 of Notice 2023-63 expressly excludes specific post-development and operational activities from the definition of software development: for internal-use software, section 5.05(1) excludes training employees to use the software, maintenance activities after the software is placed in service that do not give rise to upgrades and enhancements (such as corrective maintenance to debug, diagnose, and fix programming errors that do not add functionality or materially increase speed or efficiency), data conversion activities (except for activities to develop computer software that facilitates access to or conversion of existing data), and installation of the software (including configuration of pre-coded parameters). For software developed for sale or licensing to others, section 5.05(2) similarly excludes activities that occur after the software is ready for sale or licensing, such as marketing and promotional activities, maintenance activities that do not give rise to upgrades and enhancements, distribution activities, and customer support activities. Furthermore, section 5.04 of Notice 2023-63 explicitly states that activities associated with the purchase and installation of computer software that is purchased or leased from third parties (off-the-shelf software), including configuration of pre-coded parameters to make such software compatible with the taxpayer's business or re-engineering the business to make it compatible with the purchased software, do not constitute software development unless the taxpayer undertakes custom modifications that satisfy the definition of upgrades and enhancements.
1.4 Amortization periods and the midpoint convention

Under the TCJA version of Section 174(a)(2)(B), SRE expenditures paid or incurred in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021, and before January 1, 2025, were required to be amortized ratably over a 5-year period (60 months) in the case of domestic SRE expenditures, and over a 15-year period (180 months) in the case of any specified research or experimental expenditures which are attributable to foreign research within the meaning of Section 41(d)(4)(F) (that is, any research conducted outside the United States, the Commonwealth of Puerto Rico, or any territory or other possession of the United States). As clarified in Notice 2023-63 sections 3.03 and 3.04, whether an expenditure is domestic or foreign is determined by the physical location where the SRE activities (including software development activities) are actually performed, regardless of where the taxpayer or contract counterparty is domiciled.

Under Section 174(a)(2)(B) and Notice 2023-63 section 3.02, the amortization period begins with the midpoint of the taxable year in which the SRE expenditures are paid or incurred, regardless of the actual date or month during the taxable year when the expenditures were incurred or when the resulting software was placed in service. For a standard full 12-month taxable year, section 3.05(1) of Notice 2023-63 specifies that the midpoint is the first day of the seventh month of the taxable year (for example, July 1 for a calendar-year taxpayer), resulting in exactly 6 months of amortization allowed in the initial taxable year (6/60 or 10% for domestic expenditures; 6/180 or 3.33% for foreign expenditures), 12 months of amortization in each full subsequent taxable year during the recovery window, and the remaining 6 months of amortization in the final calendar year of the recovery cycle (Year 6 for domestic expenditures; Year 16 for foreign expenditures).
Hypothetical example 1: midpoint convention
Hypothetical. A calendar-year company pays $1,000,000 of qualifying software development costs in a full 12-month taxable year subject to the TCJA Section 174 rules.

Notice 2023-63 section 3.07 also provides a detailed worked example illustrating how the midpoint convention operates in a short taxable year: where a calendar-year corporation is formed on October 17, 2022 (creating a short first taxable year of 3 months for amortization computation purposes under section 3.05(2)) and incurs $60,000 of domestic SRE expenditures, the midpoint is November 1, 2022 (the middle of the second month, treated as the first day of that month), resulting in a deduction of $2,000 in 2022 (2/60), $12,000 in each full year from 2023 through 2026 (12/60 per year), and the remaining $10,000 in 2027 (10/60).
1.5 No recovery on disposition, retirement or abandonment

Under Section 174(d), as enacted by the TCJA, if any property with respect to which specified research or experimental expenditures are paid or incurred is disposed of, retired, or abandoned during the period during which such expenditures are allowed as an amortization deduction, no deduction shall be allowed with respect to such expenditures on account of such disposition, retirement, or abandonment, and such amortization deduction shall continue with respect to such expenditures over the remainder of the statutory 5-year or 15-year amortization period. Notice 2023-63 section 7.02 confirms this strict continuation rule, and section 7.03 specifies that the bar against immediate loss recovery applies even if the software or research project is disposed of, retired, or abandoned prior to the midpoint of the taxable year in which the expenditures were paid or incurred. Limited exceptions apply under section 7.04 only when a corporation ceases to exist in a transaction not described in IRC Section 381(a), in which case unamortized SRE expenditures generally may be deducted in the corporation's final taxable year unless thwarted by anti-abuse rules.
2. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act and Section 174A (Tax Years Beginning After December 31, 2024)
2.1 Domestic expenditures: immediate deduction restored

Public Law 119-21 (139 Stat. 72), enacted July 4, 2025, and commonly known as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA), fundamentally restructured the tax treatment of domestic research and software development costs by enacting new IRC Section 174A (Pub. L. 119-21, § 70302(a)). Under Section 174A(a), notwithstanding IRC Section 263 (which generally requires capitalization of amounts paid for permanent improvements or betterments), there shall be allowed as a deduction any domestic research or experimental expenditures which are paid or incurred by the taxpayer during the taxable year in connection with the taxpayer's trade or business. Under § 70302(e)(1) of Pub. L. 119-21, this immediate deduction applies generally to amounts paid or incurred in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024. Section 174A(b) defines "domestic research or experimental expenditures" as research or experimental expenditures paid or incurred by the taxpayer in connection with the taxpayer's trade or business that are not attributable to foreign research (within the meaning of Section 41(d)(4)(F)). Critically, Section 174A(d) explicitly preserves the software rule for domestic costs: for purposes of Section 174A, any amount paid or incurred in connection with the development of any software shall be treated as a research or experimental expenditure. Unlike temporary tax provisions enacted under prior reconciliation bills, Section 174A contains no statutory sunset date, restoring immediate expensing for domestic software development on a permanent basis.

Under § 70302(c) of Pub. L. 119-21 and Rev. Proc. 2025-28 section 7, the transition to Section 174A for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024, is treated by statute as a change in method of accounting initiated by the taxpayer, made with the consent of the Secretary of the Treasury, and applied on a cut-off basis for domestic research or experimental expenditures paid or incurred in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024, with no IRC Section 481(a) adjustment.
2.2 Foreign expenditures: 15-year amortization retained

Concurrently with the enactment of Section 174A for domestic costs, § 70302(b) of Pub. L. 119-21 amended IRC Section 174 (retitled "Amortization of Foreign Research and Experimental Expenditures") so that Section 174(a) now governs exclusively foreign research or experimental expenditures—defined under amended Section 174(b) as research or experimental expenditures paid or incurred in connection with the taxpayer's trade or business which are attributable to foreign research within the meaning of Section 41(d)(4)(F). Under amended Section 174(a)(2), foreign research or experimental expenditures (which continue to include foreign software development costs under Section 174(c)(3)) must still be charged to capital account and amortized ratably over a 15-year period (180 months) beginning with the midpoint of the taxable year in which such expenditures are paid or incurred. Software developed through engineering or programming activities performed outside the United States, Puerto Rico, and U.S. territories therefore continues to follow the mandatory 180-month amortization schedule illustrated in Example 1.

Furthermore, Pub. L. 119-21 amended Section 174(d) (relating to the treatment upon disposition, retirement, or abandonment of property tied to foreign research expenditures) to insert the phrase "and no reduction to amount realized" after "no deduction." Consequently, when property with respect to which foreign research or experimental expenditures were paid or incurred is sold, disposed of, retired, or abandoned during the 15-year amortization window, the taxpayer is barred not only from claiming an abandonment or retirement loss deduction, but also from applying the unamortized foreign SRE basis to reduce the amount realized (or offset gain) upon a taxable sale or exchange. Under § 70302(e)(2) of Pub. L. 119-21, this strengthened anti-recovery rule in Section 174(d) applies to property disposed of, retired, or abandoned after May 12, 2025.

body.text: 2.3 Elective amortization of domestic costs

Section 174A(c). Although Section 174A(a) restores immediate expensing as the default rule for domestic research and software development expenditures, taxpayers with net operating losses, international minimum tax exposure, or specific income-smoothing objectives may prefer to defer deductions. Under Section 174A(c)(1), at the election of the taxpayer, domestic research or experimental expenditures which would (but for Section 174A) be chargeable to capital account but are not chargeable to property of a character subject to depreciation under Section 167 or depletion under Section 611 may be treated as deferred expenses and amortized ratably over such period of not less than 60 months as may be selected by the taxpayer, beginning with the month in which the taxpayer first realizes benefits from such expenditures. Under Section 174A(c)(2), this election may be made for any taxable year, but must be made not later than the time prescribed by law for filing the return for such taxable year (including extensions thereof). Once elected, both the method of charging domestic expenditures to capital account and the amortization period selected by the taxpayer must be adhered to in computing taxable income for the election year and for all subsequent taxable years unless, with the approval of the Secretary of the Treasury, a change to a different method (or to a different period) is authorized with respect to part or all of such expenditures. The election under Section 174A(c) does not apply to any item paid or incurred during any taxable year before the taxable year for which the election is made.

Rev. Proc. 2025-28 section 6 sets forth the administrative procedures for making a Section 174A(c) election (when not executed as an accounting method change). Under section 6.02 of Rev. Proc. 2025-28, the taxpayer makes the election by attaching a statement titled "FILED PURSUANT TO SECTION 6.02 OF REV. PROC. 2025-28" to its timely filed original federal income tax return (including extensions) for the first taxable year to which the election applies, identifying the taxpayer, declaring that the taxpayer is charging domestic research or experimental expenditures to a capital account under Section 174A(c), and specifying the chosen amortization period of not less than 60 months. Under section 6.01 of Rev. Proc. 2025-28, an initial election under Section 174A(c) applies to all domestic research or experimental expenditures paid or incurred by the taxpayer during the election year and subsequent years unless IRS consent to change is obtained.

Section 59(e). As an alternative to both immediate deduction under Section 174A(a) and 60-month-minimum amortization from the month of benefit realization under Section 174A(c), Pub. L. 119-21 (§ 70302(d)) updated the cross-reference in IRC Section 59(e)(2)(B) to refer to an expenditure deductible under Section 174A(a) (replacing the prior reference to Section 174(a)). Under Section 59(e)(1), a taxpayer may elect to deduct any qualified expenditure ratably over the 10-year period beginning with the taxable year in which such expenditure was made (without waiting for the month in which benefits are first realized, and without applying the Section 174 midpoint convention). Under Section 59(e)(4)(A) and Treas. Reg. § 1.59-1(b)(1), an election under Section 59(e) may be made with respect to any specific dollar portion of any qualified expenditure (providing dollar-by-dollar flexibility rather than an all-or-nothing mandate), and under Section 59(e)(4)(B) an election made with respect to an expenditure for a given taxable year may be revoked only with the consent of the Secretary.

While the statutory text of Section 59(e)(4) explicitly provides that an election may be made for "any portion of any qualified expenditure" and is irrevocable for that elected expenditure without IRS consent—without using the exact phrase "annual basis" in the Code section itself—Treasury Regulation § 1.59-1(b)(1) confirms that a Section 59(e) election applies only to the specific qualified expenditures (or designated dollar portion thereof) paid or incurred in the taxable year for which the election is made, and does not bind the taxpayer to elect Section 59(e) for expenditures paid or incurred in subsequent taxable years.
3. Transition Rules for 2022–2024 Domestic Costs
3.1 All taxpayers: recovery of unamortized amounts

Because domestic software development costs paid or incurred in taxable years beginning in 2022, 2023, and 2024 were required to be capitalized over 60 months under the TCJA version of Section 174, virtually all taxpayers entered the 2025 taxable year carrying substantial unamortized balances of 2022–2024 domestic SRE expenditures. Under § 70302(f)(2) of Pub. L. 119-21, any taxpayer (regardless of gross receipts size) that was required to capitalize domestic research or experimental expenditures paid or incurred in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021, and before January 1, 2025, may elect to deduct any remaining unamortized amount with respect to such expenditures either:

items: (i) in full in the first taxable year beginning after December 31, 2024 (e.g., the 2025 taxable year for a calendar-year taxpayer), or
(ii) ratably over the 2-taxable-year period beginning with the first taxable year beginning after December 31, 2024 (e.g., 50% in 2025 and 50% in 2026 for a calendar-year taxpayer).

body.text: If a taxpayer does not make this acceleration election under § 70302(f)(2) (and, if eligible, does not make the small business retroactive election under § 70302(f)(1)), the taxpayer defaults to continuing to amortize its 2022–2024 domestic SRE expenditures ratably over the remainder of their original 60-month amortization schedules. Under § 70302(f)(2)(B) and Rev. Proc. 2025-28 (which modifies section 7.02 of Rev. Proc. 2025-23, the List of Automatic Changes), this election to accelerate unamortized 2022–2024 domestic costs is treated as an automatic change in method of accounting under IRC Sections 446(e) and 481, implemented on a cut-off basis with the first taxable year beginning after December 31, 2024, designated as the year of change, using a streamlined statement filed in lieu of Form 3115 (Application for Change in Accounting Method) under section 7.02(3)(d) and (5) of Rev. Proc. 2025-23 as modified by Rev. Proc. 2025-28.
Hypothetical example 2: unamortized 2023 domestic costs

Hypothetical. A calendar-year corporation capitalized $600,000 of domestic software development costs in 2023. Applying the TCJA 60-month schedule and midpoint convention, it deducted $60,000 in 2023 (6/60) and $120,000 in 2024 (12/60), leaving $600,000 − $60,000 − $120,000 = $420,000 of unamortized domestic software costs at the start of 2025.
3.2 Deemed method changes for early-filed returns

Because Pub. L. 119-21 was enacted on July 4, 2025, and Rev. Proc. 2025-28 was released on August 28, 2025, certain fiscal-year or short-year taxpayers with a first taxable year beginning after December 31, 2024, faced return filing deadlines shortly after the revenue procedure's release. Rev. Proc. 2025-28 (modifying section 7.02(6) of Rev. Proc. 2025-23) establishes the exact parameters of this relief: under section 7.02(6)(a), a taxpayer that filed its federal income tax return on or before September 15, 2025, for a taxable year beginning after December 31, 2024, is deemed to have complied with the automatic accounting method change procedures to adopt Section 174A if the taxpayer either (i) deducted domestic research or experimental expenditures under Section 174A(a) on that return, or (ii) charged such expenditures to capital account and amortized them under Section 174A(c) and properly reported such amortization on Form 4562 (Depreciation and Amortization), Part VI. Similarly, under section 7.02(6)(b), a taxpayer that filed such an early return on or before September 15, 2025, and deducted either the full remaining unamortized 2022–2024 domestic SRE amount or a ratable one-half portion thereof on that return is deemed to have complied with the method-change rules for the § 70302(f)(2) recovery election without having attached the formal Rev. Proc. 2025-28 transition statement.
3.3 Small business taxpayers: retroactive application

While large taxpayers are limited to forward-looking recovery starting in their first taxable year beginning after December 31, 2024, Congress enacted special retroactive relief for qualifying small businesses. Under § 70302(f)(1) of Pub. L. 119-21, an "eligible taxpayer"—defined as any taxpayer (other than a tax shelter prohibited from using the cash method under IRC Section 448(a)(3)) that meets the gross receipts test of IRC Section 448(c) for its first taxable year beginning after December 31, 2024—may elect to have the amendments made by § 70302 (including immediate domestic expensing under Section 174A) apply retroactively to amounts paid or incurred in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021. Under section 3.01(1) of Rev. Proc. 2025-28, an eligible small business making this retroactive election may either deduct its 2022–2024 domestic research and software development expenditures in the applicable taxable year paid or incurred under Section 174A(a) or charge them to capital account and amortize them over at least 60 months under Section 174A(c).

items: All-or-nothing consistency rule: Under section 3.03(1) of Rev. Proc. 2025-28, once an eligible small business taxpayer makes the retroactive § 70302(f)(1) election for any one applicable taxable year, the taxpayer must apply the election consistently to all applicable taxable years (all taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021, and before January 1, 2025) in which the taxpayer paid or incurred domestic research or experimental expenditures.

Statutory deadline: Under § 70302(f)(1)(B) of Pub. L. 119-21, the retroactive election had to be made within one year of the date of enactment (July 4, 2025). Because July 4, 2026, fell on a Saturday (and was a legal holiday), Rev. Proc. 2025-28 sections 2.06(2) and 3.03(3) established the final deadline (pursuant to IRC Section 7503) as Monday, July 6, 2026, or, if earlier with respect to a specific prior taxable year, the expiration of the period of limitations for filing a claim for credit or refund under IRC Section 6511(a) for that taxable year. Note: As of November 11, 2026, the July 6, 2026 deadline for small business retroactive amended-return elections under § 70302(f)(1) has expired.

Procedural mechanics (Amended Returns, AARs, or Accounting Method Change): Under section 3.03(2) of Rev. Proc. 2025-28, an eligible small business making the retroactive election via return filings was required to attach a statement titled "FILED PURSUANT TO SECTION 3.03 OF REV. PROC. 2025-28" to its original return, amended return (e.g., Form 1120-X or Form 1040-X), or partnership Administrative Adjustment Request (AAR under IRC Section 6227) for each applicable taxable year. Under section 3.03(4), an original return for an applicable taxable year (such as an extended 2024 return) timely filed on or before November 15, 2025, that deducted domestic research or experimental expenditures was deemed to have validly made the § 70302(f)(1) election for that year without the formal statement, provided the taxpayer timely filed amended returns or AARs for its earlier 2022 and 2023 applicable years. Alternatively, rather than filing multiple amended returns or AARs for 2022–2024, Rev. Proc. 2025-28 section 7 (modifying section 7.02(3)(c) of Rev. Proc. 2025-23) permitted an eligible small business to implement the retroactive § 70302(f)(1) election as an automatic change in method of accounting on its 2024 or 2025 return using a modified IRC Section 481(a) adjustment (provided the change was made in connection with a timely § 70302(f)(1) election by July 6, 2026).

Superseding return relief for 2024 returns: Under section 8.01 of Rev. Proc. 2025-28, eligible small business partnerships, S corporations, C corporations, individuals, trusts, estates, and exempt organizations that had already timely filed their 2024 tax returns prior to the issuance of Rev. Proc. 2025-28 without an extension (or whose extended due date fell before September 15, 2025) were granted an automatic six-month extension of time from the unextended due date to file a superseding 2024 tax return to apply the retroactive Section 174A rules directly on that superseding return.

body.text: From a statutory perspective, § 70302(f)(1) of Pub. L. 119-21 and sections 3 through 5 of Rev. Proc. 2025-28 grant the retroactive pre-2025 election exclusively to "eligible taxpayers" satisfying the Section 448(c) $31 million gross receipts test; for taxpayers exceeding $31 million in average gross receipts, the TCJA version of Section 174 remains the governing law for taxable years beginning in 2022, 2023, and 2024, meaning those taxpayers have no statutory authority to deduct 2022–2024 domestic SRE costs on amended 2022–2024 returns and must instead use the forward-looking recovery election in § 70302(f)(2) starting in 2025.
4. Interaction With the Section 41 Research Credit
4.1 Section 174 status is a prerequisite for qualified research

Under IRC Section 41(d)(1) (as amended by Pub. L. 119-21, § 70302(d) to reference Section 174A), research activities constitute "qualified research" eligible for the federal Research and Development (R&D) tax credit only if four cumulative statutory requirements (commonly known as the Four-Part Test, detailed in Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)) are satisfied with respect to each separate business component:

items: The Section 174 / Section 174A Test (§ 41(d)(1)(A) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(2)(i)): The expenditures with respect to such research must be eligible to be treated as domestic research or experimental expenditures under Section 174A (or Section 174 for pre-2025 years);

The Technological Information Test (§ 41(d)(1)(B)(i) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(3)): The research must be undertaken for the purpose of discovering information which is technological in nature (meaning the process of experimentation fundamentally relies on the principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science);

The Business Component / Permitted Purpose Test (§ 41(d)(1)(B)(ii) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(5)): The application of that technological information must be intended to be useful in the development of a new or improved business component of the taxpayer (defined as a product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention to be held for sale, lease, or license, or used by the taxpayer in its trade or business) for a qualified purpose—namely, a new or improved function, performance, or reliability or quality (whereas research relating to style, taste, cosmetic, or seasonal design factors is expressly disqualified under Section 41(d)(3)(B)); and

The Process of Experimentation Test (§ 41(d)(1)(C) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(4), (6)): Substantially all (defined in Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6) as 80% or more) of the research activities measured on a cost or other consistently applied reasonable basis must constitute elements of a process of experimentation designed to evaluate one or more alternatives to capability, method, or appropriate design uncertainty.

body.text: Furthermore, even when a software project satisfies all four elements of Section 41(d)(1), the Section 41 credit applies only to strictly enumerated categories of Qualified Research Expenses (QREs) under Section 41(b): in-house W-2 wages paid for qualified services (engaging in, directly supervising, or directly supporting qualified research), supplies used in the conduct of qualified research, computer rental or cloud hosting costs used directly in conducting qualified research under Section 41(b)(2)(A)(iii), and 65% (or 75% / 100% for certain consortia and energy research) of contract research expenses under Section 41(b)(3). By contrast, Section 174 and Section 174A encompass a significantly wider pool of software development activities (including routine coding, requirement documentation, and quality assurance testing that may not involve technological uncertainty or a formal process of experimentation) as well as broader indirect cost allocations (such as depreciation, rent, utilities, and patent legal fees under Notice 2023-63 section 4.03) that are ineligible for the Section 41 credit.
4.2 Internal-use software

Under IRC Section 41(d)(4)(E), except to the extent provided by Treasury regulations, research with respect to computer software which is developed by (or for the benefit of) the taxpayer primarily for internal use by the taxpayer is excluded from qualified research for purposes of the Section 41 credit (unless the software is developed for use in an activity that itself constitutes qualified research or in a production process that meets the requirements of Section 41(d)(1)). Under the final Treasury regulations in Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(6), software is NOT treated as developed primarily for internal use if it is developed to be commercially sold, leased, licensed, or otherwise marketed to third parties, or if it is developed to enable the taxpayer to interact with third parties or to allow third parties to initiate functions or review data on the taxpayer's system (the "third-party subset" or "dual-function" rules). If software is developed primarily for the taxpayer's internal use (such as general and administrative software covering financial management, human resources, and support services), it qualifies for the Section 41 credit only if, in addition to satisfying the general Four-Part Test of Section 41(d)(1), it also satisfies the stringent High Threshold of Innovation Test under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(6)(vii):

items: Innovative (§ 1.41-4(c)(6)(vii)(A)-(B)): The software is innovative in that the software would result in a reduction in cost or improvement in speed or other measurable improvement, that is substantial and economically significant, if the development is or would have been successful;

Significant Economic Risk (§ 1.41-4(c)(6)(vii)(A), (C)): The software development involves significant economic risk in that the taxpayer commits substantial resources to the development and there is substantial uncertainty, because of technical risk, that such resources would be recovered within a reasonable period; and

Not Commercially Available (§ 1.41-4(c)(6)(vii)(A), (D)): The software is not commercially available for use by the taxpayer in that the software cannot be purchased, leased, or licensed and used for the intended purpose without modifications that would satisfy the innovation and significant economic risk requirements.

body.text: Under the exact text of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(6)(vii), the phrase "substantial and economically significant" is the metric defining the first prong ("Innovative"), whereas the second prong is expressly titled and defined as "Significant economic risk" (requiring substantial committed resources and substantial technical uncertainty of recovery within a reasonable period).
4.3 Section 280C(c) coordination

To prevent taxpayers from claiming both a full tax deduction (or full capital basis recovery) and a full tax credit on the exact same dollar of research expenditure, IRC Section 280C(c) requires coordination between Section 174/174A and the Section 41 research credit. During the 2022–2024 TCJA window, former Section 280C(c)(1) contained a modified rule providing that the capitalized amount under Section 174 was reduced only to the extent that the Section 41(a) research credit exceeded the amount allowable as an amortization deduction for that taxable year.

Pub. L. 119-21 (§ 70302(d)(2)) repealed that TCJA formulation and restored the classic dollar-for-dollar reduction rule for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024. Under amended Section 280C(c)(1), any domestic research or experimental expenditures otherwise taken into account under Section 174A (whether currently deducted under Section 174A(a) or charged to capital account and amortized under Section 174A(c) or Section 59(e)) shall be reduced by the full amount of the credit determined under Section 41(a) for the taxable year. Alternatively, to avoid reducing its Section 174A deduction (or capital account) and to simplify state tax return computations, a taxpayer may elect under Section 280C(c)(2) on a timely filed return (including extensions) to claim a reduced Section 41 research credit for the taxable year. Under Section 280C(c)(2)(B), the reduced credit equals the full gross Section 41(a) credit minus the product of (i) the full Section 41(a) credit and (ii) the maximum corporate income tax rate in effect under IRC Section 11(b) (currently 21%, meaning the taxpayer retains 79% of the gross credit while preserving 100% of its Section 174A deduction). Once made for a taxable year, a Section 280C(c)(2) election is irrevocable for that year—with one critical transitional exception: for eligible small business taxpayers that made the retroactive § 70302(f)(1) election to apply Section 174A to their 2022–2024 taxable years, sections 4 and 5 of Rev. Proc. 2025-28 granted special authority to make a late Section 280C(c)(2) reduced-credit election (if not previously made) or to revoke a previously made Section 280C(c)(2) election for any applicable 2022–2024 taxable year on an amended return or AAR filed on or before the July 6, 2026 deadline.

Under Section 280C(c)(1), domestic research or experimental expenditures are reduced dollar for dollar by 100% of the amount of the Section 41(a) credit claimed (unless the taxpayer elects the 21% reduced credit under Section 280C(c)(2)).

Under Section 41(c)(4)(A), a taxpayer electing the ASC calculates a gross credit equal to 14% of so much of the taxpayer's QREs for the taxable year as exceeds 50% of the average QREs for the 3 taxable years preceding the credit determination year. Under Section 41(c)(4)(B), the 6% rate (applied to 100% of current-year QREs with no base subtraction) applies only if the taxpayer has no qualified research expenses in any one of the 3 taxable years preceding the taxable year for which the credit is being determined. Thus, whether the 6% rate or the 14% rate applies depends strictly on whether the taxpayer incurred positive QREs in each of the three preceding taxable years—NOT on how many years the taxpayer has claimed the credit on a tax return. A company that incurred QREs in each of the prior three years uses the 14% rate even in the very first year it claims the Section 41 credit; conversely, a startup with zero QREs in Year 1 uses the 6% rate in Years 1, 2, and 3, and transitions to the 14% formula in Year 4 once it has three full preceding years with positive QREs.
5. Book-Tax Differences Under GAAP

Under ASC 985-20, all software development costs incurred prior to establishing "technological feasibility" (achieved via a detail program design or a working model) are expensed as R&D for financial reporting purposes, and costs incurred after technological feasibility is established up until general release to customers are capitalized. Under the historical framework of ASC 350-40, projects were divided into three sequential stages: (1) the Preliminary Project Stage (expensed), (2) the Application Development Stage (capitalized), and (3) the Post-Implementation/Operation Stage (expensed).

Directly responsive to the prevalence of nonlinear, iterative Agile software development methodologies (in which teams develop software in short sprints rather than linear waterfall phases), ASU 2025-06 supersedes and removes all references to sequential project stages throughout ASC 350-40. In place of project stages, ASU 2025-06 establishes a single, method-neutral capitalization starting threshold: an entity begins capitalizing internal-use software costs when both (1) management with the relevant authority has authorized and committed to funding the software project, and (2) it is probable that the project will be completed and the software will be used to perform the function intended (referred to as the "probable-to-complete recognition threshold"). If substantial uncertainty exists regarding the development of novel, unique, or unproven software functionality ("significant development uncertainty"), the probable-to-complete threshold is not met and costs are expensed until that uncertainty is resolved. ASU 2025-06 takes effect for all entities for annual reporting periods beginning after December 15, 2027 (including interim periods within those annual periods), with early adoption permitted as of the beginning of an annual reporting period, while leaving ASC 985-20 unchanged.

Analysis of Book-Tax Timing Differences: During the 2022–2024 TCJA window, Section 174 required mandatory tax capitalization over 5 years (domestic) or 15 years (foreign) for virtually all software planning, design, coding, and testing costs regardless of whether those costs were expensed on the financial statements under ASC 985-20 (prior to technological feasibility) or ASC 350-40, generating large Deferred Tax Assets (DTAs) and book-tax timing mismatches. For taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024, under Section 174A, these book-tax differences persist (1) in reverse whenever an entity capitalizes domestic internal-use software costs on its GAAP balance sheet under ASC 350-40 while immediately deducting 100% of those domestic software costs on its tax return under Section 174A(a) (creating a Deferred Tax Liability), (2) for all foreign software development costs, which remain subject to 15-year tax amortization under Section 174(a) while frequently being expensed for book purposes, and (3) whenever a taxpayer elects 60-month-minimum amortization under Section 174A(c) or 10-year amortization under Section 59(e).
6. Effects on Other Tax Calculations (International and Corporate Tax Interplay)

items: Foreign Tax Credits (IRC §§ 861 and 904): Under Treas. Reg. § 1.861-17, research and experimental expenditures (including software development deductions under Section 174/174A) are allocated to broad product categories and apportioned between U.S.-source income and foreign-source income (in the relevant Section 904 foreign tax credit baskets). Because apportioned R&D deductions reduce the numerator of the Section 904 foreign-source taxable income fraction (Foreign-Source Taxable Income ÷ Worldwide Taxable Income), a larger current-year R&D deduction reduces foreign-source taxable income and tightens (reduces) the Section 904 Foreign Tax Credit limitation. Conversely, when R&D and software development costs are capitalized and amortized over 5 or 15 years rather than deducted immediately, a smaller R&D deduction is apportioned against foreign-source income in the initial year, which increases foreign-source taxable income and generally eases (increases) the taxpayer's Section 904 Foreign Tax Credit limitation in that initial year (Conversely, restoring immediate 100% domestic expensing under Section 174A in 2025 increases the current-year R&D deduction apportioned under Treas. Reg. § 1.861-17, which can reduce foreign-source taxable income and tighten the FTC limitation).

Foreign-Derived Intangible Income / FDII (IRC § 250): Under Section 250, a domestic C corporation's FDII deduction is tied to its "Deduction Eligible Income" (DEI), which equals gross income (excluding specified foreign branches, GILTI/NCTI, etc.) minus allocable deductions (including Section 174/174A R&D and software amortization deductions).

Base Erosion and Anti-Abuse Tax / BEAT (IRC § 59A): Under Section 59A, an applicable large corporation owes BEAT only to the extent that the BEAT rate (10%, or 10.5% as amended for future periods) applied to "Modified Taxable Income" (regular taxable income plus deductible base erosion payments made to foreign related parties) exceeds the corporation's regular tax liability reduced by certain credits (importantly, the Section 41 R&D credit does not reduce regular tax for BEAT comparison purposes under Section 59A(b)(1)(B)).

7. Audit Scrutiny and Substantiation Standards

While the IRS possesses general statutory examination authority under IRC Section 7602 to examine books, records, and cost classifications for any open taxable year within the Section 6501 statute of limitations, no provision in the TCJA, Pub. L. 119-21, Notice 2023-63, or Rev. Proc. 2025-28 grants a special new statutory authorization to retroactively reclassify pre-2022 software development costs under post-2021 standards. On the contrary, section 1 of Notice 2023-63 explicitly states: "The guidance in this notice does not apply for purposes of determining whether an expenditure paid or incurred for taxable years beginning before January 1, 2022, is a research or experimental expenditure under § 174 as in effect for taxable years beginning before January 1, 2022 (former § 174)." Furthermore, section 7.01 of Rev. Proc. 2025-23 (and prior automatic accounting method change guidance in Rev. Proc. 2023-11) expressly provides that the cut-off change to TCJA Section 174 for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021, does not provide audit protection for expenditures paid or incurred in taxable years beginning before January 1, 2022, while simultaneously confirming that pre-2022 years remain governed strictly by former Section 174 and Rev. Proc. 2000-50. For taxable years beginning in 2022 and thereafter, however, taxpayers claiming either the Section 41 R&D credit, the § 70302(f)(1) small business retroactive election, the § 70302(f)(2) unamortized recovery election, or immediate domestic expensing under Section 174A(a) vs. 15-year foreign amortization under Section 174(a) must maintain contemporaneous project accounting records, geographic labor tracking (to substantiate domestic versus foreign research locations under Notice 2023-63 section 3.04), and clear delineation between qualifying software development activities (section 5.03) and non-qualifying maintenance or configuration costs (sections 5.04–5.05).
